teaching.causalExplanation: Let's launch them together. The low one arrives after about two point six seven seconds. The high one is still up there. It finally lands after about five point five one seconds, in exactly the same spot. Same speed, same target, two angles, two very different flights. So why are there two angles, and how do we find them both? For level ground we already have a shortcut, the range equation. R equals u squared sin two theta over g. Remember its conditions: launch and landing at the same height, no air resistance, and constant g. It can run backwards, too. Say a projectile launched at thirty-eight degrees lands forty-five metres away on level ground. Rearrange for u: u is the square root of R g over sin two theta. That's the square root of four hundred and forty-one over sin seventy-six degrees, about twenty-one point three metres per second. Now our target. This time we know u and R, and we want theta. Rearranging, sin two theta equals R g over u squared. That's seventy-two times nine point eight over nine hundred, which is zero point seven eight four. Your calculator's inverse sine gives two theta as fifty-one point six degrees, so theta is twenty-five point eight degrees. That's the low path. But the calculator only gave us one answer. Where's the other?

scenes.teachingReason: Look at the sine graph from zero to one hundred and eighty degrees. It rises to one at ninety degrees, then falls back again, symmetrically. scenes.teachingReason: The range is biggest when sin two theta is one, at forty-five degrees. So the minimum speed satisfies R equals u squared over g, and u is the square root of twenty times nine point eight, the square root of one hundred and ninety-six, exactly fourteen point zero metres per second. Any slower, and the sine would have to be bigger than one. The slip is to aim at ninety degrees because it makes sin theta biggest. Straight up has no range at all. It's sin two theta that matters.
